coverage.headline: Little Drama at Anthropic's Settlement Hearing
Anthropic Settlement Appears to Cruise Through Its Final Fairness Hearing
Firms Cut From $101M Anthropic Atty Fees Appeal To 9th Circ.
coverage.summary: Two law firms involved in securing Anthropic's $1.5 billion copyright settlement appealed to the Ninth Circuit after being excluded from attorney fees awarded solely to court-appointed class counsel. The appeal follows the July 20 final approval order that set attorney fees at approximately $101.5 million.

coverage.headline: Firms Appeal After Exclusion From Fees Award in Anthropic Case
coverage.summary: Edelson and Oppenheim + Zebrak appealed to the Ninth Circuit after being cut out of the $101 million attorney fee award in the Bartz v. Anthropic settlement, which was restricted to court-approved class counsel Susman Godfrey and Lieff Cabraser. The two firms were among those previously castigated by Judge Alsup over an improper initial $300 million fees request.

coverage.headline: The Bartz/Anthropic Settlement is still a hot mess but at least it is the largest known copyright recovery of all time (for piracy)?
coverage.summary: IPKat analyzes the July 20 final approval of the $1.5 billion settlement, noting that 440,490 of the 482,460 eligible works had claims filed and characterizing the outcome as complex and contested despite its record size. The piece situates the settlement in the broader AI copyright litigation landscape.

coverage.headline: Bartz v Anthropic: When to Expect Payments, Next Steps
coverage.summary: Class counsel confirmed that class members will not begin receiving payments until at least end of 2026, with disbursement contingent on whether any appeals are filed before the August 19 deadline; payments will be made in two stages (roughly 70%/30%) as Anthropic pays in installments through September 2027.

coverage.headline: Federal Court Approves $1.5 Billion Anthropic Copyright Settlement — Largest in History
coverage.summary: Analysis of the July 20 final approval order in Bartz v. Anthropic PBC (No. 3:24-cv-05417-AMO), confirming Anthropic's obligation to pay $1.5 billion plus interest to copyright owners whose works were downloaded from pirated datasets LibGen and PiLiMi to train its large language models.

coverage.headline: Anthropic's $1.5 billion copyright settlement gets final approval but authors aren't cheering
coverage.summary: Judge Martínez-Olguín granted final approval of the settlement on July 20, 2026, with authors set to receive approximately $3,100 per work while over $100 million went to lawyers and Anthropic admitted no wrongdoing. The case sets a financial benchmark for AI copyright claims but creates no binding legal precedent on the fair use question.

coverage.headline: Anthropic AI copyright infringement lawsuit isn't a total win for authors
coverage.summary: NPR examines the mixed outcomes of the Bartz v. Anthropic $1.5 billion settlement, noting that thousands of authors must split the fund with publishers and that over $100 million went to plaintiffs' lawyers, with some observers viewing the result as more favorable to AI companies than to the publishing industry.

coverage.headline: The Landmark $1.5 Billion Anthropic Settlement Wins Final Approval
coverage.summary: Analysis of the July 20 final approval order in Bartz v. Anthropic, noting the judge found the settlement 'fair, reasonable, and adequate' and that success at trial was not assured. Publishers stand to receive tens of millions of dollars after being added to the class as beneficial copyright owners.

coverage.headline: Anthropic Settlement Update: Final Settlement Approved
coverage.source: Writer Beware (Science Fiction & Fantasy Writers Association)
coverage.summary: Confirmed Judge Martínez-Olguín's July 20 final approval of the $1.5 billion settlement, described as the largest copyright infringement recovery ever, with the distribution process now proceeding subject to the appeal window.

coverage.headline: Bartz v Anthropic Granted Final Approval by the Court
coverage.summary: TAA reported that Judge Martínez-Olguín called the settlement 'fair, reasonable, and adequate' and overruled all 53 objections, with class counsel reporting a 91.3% claims rate and only 350 valid opt-outs representing 1,802 works. The post details the court-ordered dispute resolution process going forward, including referral of unresolved claims disputes to a Special Master.

coverage.headline: Judge approves record $1.5 billion AI copyright settlement involving Anthropic
coverage.summary: The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California granted final approval to the $1.5 billion Bartz v. Anthropic settlement on July 20, 2026, resolving allegations that Anthropic used pirated books to train its Claude AI platform; the case had previously seen a key ruling that legally purchased books could be used for AI training but pirated copies could not.

coverage.headline: Anthropic Settlement Receives Final Approval
coverage.summary: Locus reported, citing Bloomberg, that the Bartz v. Anthropic settlement is 'the largest copyright class action settlement in US history,' paying about $3,100 per author across more than 480,000 works, with $122 million going toward attorneys and litigation costs.

coverage.headline: Anthropic to pay €1.3bn in biggest copyright settlement on record
coverage.summary: A U.S. federal judge approved the $1.5 billion settlement between Anthropic and a class of authors, marking the largest copyright class action in U.S. history and the first major resolution of a wave of lawsuits against AI companies over book training data. Judge Martínez-Olguín rejected objections from some authors who argued the payout was too small.

coverage.headline: Anthropic copyright settlement gets final approval: $3,000 per book, no binding precedent
coverage.summary: Following final court approval of the Bartz v. Anthropic settlement, class members stand to receive approximately $3,000 per work for Anthropic's unauthorized downloading of books from shadow libraries LibGen and PiLiMi. Because Anthropic denied wrongdoing and the case settled before trial, the ruling sets no binding legal precedent on AI fair use.

coverage.headline: Bartz v. Anthropic Settlement Receives Final Approval
coverage.summary: Authors Alliance reported that Judge Martínez-Olguín's 23-page final approval order closes the case and establishes that payments begin one business day after the 'Effective Date'—defined as expiration of the 30-day Ninth Circuit appeal window. The court reminded non-class objectors they remain free to bring independent claims.

coverage.headline: Bartz v. Anthropic Settlement Receives Final Approval
coverage.summary: Authors Alliance reports that Judge Martínez-Olguín closed the case with a 23-page final approval order covering settlement administration details and attorneys' fees, noting the court declined to entertain objections from non-class members while reminding them they remain free to bring their own claims.

coverage.headline: Bartz et al v. Anthropic PBC – Final Approval Coverage
coverage.summary: Law360's case page documents the lead-up to and grant of final approval of Anthropic's $1.5 billion copyright settlement with authors, including coverage of the fairness hearing where class counsel defended a $187.5 million attorney fee request as justified by the settlement they created.

coverage.headline: Anthropic, Authors' $1.5 Billion Deal Earns Final Approval
coverage.summary: A California federal judge gave final approval to Anthropic's $1.5 billion copyright class action settlement with authors, setting aside roughly $101.5 million in attorney fees for class counsel. The case, Bartz v. Anthropic PBC, is described as the largest copyright class action settlement in U.S. history.

coverage.headline: Court Grants Final Approval of $1.5 Billion Anthropic Copyright Settlement
coverage.summary: Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín granted final approval of the $1.5 billion Bartz v. Anthropic settlement on July 20, 2026, overruling all 53 objections and entering final judgment. The court trimmed class representative service awards from $50,000 to $15,000 each and approved roughly $101.5 million in attorney fees, with all unspent funds remaining in a non-reversionary pool for authors.
